_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: With regard to a firstborn it is stated, “you shall not redeem”: it has no redemption by which the redemption money would take on its sanctity and it would go out to non-sacred status.
rashi:a1.2: But it may be sold: and it is eaten in sanctity. And this is its sanctity: that one may not slaughter it in the butchers’ market and may not weigh it by the litra.
rashi:a1.3: Say the latter clause: of the verse of “you shall not redeem.”
rashi:a2.1: The first clause of the verse is with regard to a blemished animal: that is why we infer “but it may be sold”; and its latter clause, where it is written “and you shall sprinkle their blood,” is with regard to an unblemished one.
rashi:a4.1: With her maidservant’s offspring: and it is not known which one is the priest and which one is the slave.
rashi:a4.2: They free each other: each one writes, “If I am the master and you are the slave, you are hereby a free man,” and then both will be permitted to marry a Jewish woman.
rashi:a4.3: And they both partake of teruma: as long as they have not freed each other, since the slave of a priest also eats teruma.
rashi:a4.4: And they receive one share in the granary: that is to say, when the two are together, teruma is given to them at the threshing floors; but to one of them alone no share is given until his fellow comes, since perhaps this one is the slave. And this tanna holds that teruma is not distributed to a slave unless his master is with him, lest people come to raise him to [priestly] lineage.
rashi:a4.5: And their firstborn: of these comingled ones. If a firstborn animal was born in their flock, it grazes, etc., as [the Gemara] explains.
rashi:a5.1: What is different about ours from theirs? Ours too: have no remedy until they are blemished. At this point the one raising the objection had not considered the latter clause, which teaches that it is eaten with its blemish by the owners, whereas ours we would give to a priest with its blemish. And Rav Naḥman answers it this way at the conclusion of the matter.
rashi:a5.2: Rather, is it not when the Temple is standing: and ours we would give to the priest to sacrifice, whereas theirs they acquire for themselves. Even though a priest’s animal is also subject to the firstborn obligation, as we say in Bekhorot, in the mishna of the second chapter (13a), [that priests and Levites] were exempted only from the redemption of the son and of the firstborn donkey, these graze. For with other firstborns a priest loses nothing, since he himself sacrifices the sacrificial portions of the firstborn and eats it. But with these, where one of them is a non-priest, if he gave their firstborn to be sacrificed they could no longer eat of it, since an unblemished firstborn while the Temple stands is not eaten by non-priests, as we say in Eizehu Mekoman (Zevaḥim 56b): the firstborn is eaten by priests. Therefore it grazes, and when it becomes unfit he eats it with its blemish, since each one says to the priest: I am a priest, and I will eat the firstborn. For once a blemish has befallen it, there is only the prohibition of robbery; and here there is not even a prohibition of robbery, since perhaps this one is a priest and acquired it, and the burden of proof rests on the one who seeks to take from his fellow.
rashi:a5.3: Well: for this reason he has the power to keep it and say: perhaps I am a priest and acquired it first, and I will not give it to a priest; and I will wait until I can eat it.
rashi:a5.4: But if you say it does not: if the priest has no acquisition in a firstborn during its lifetime, why do we let him remove it from the altar? Let the treasurer come and take it and give it to a proper priest, since there is no acquisition in it except from the altar onward. Rather, he certainly has acquisition during its lifetime in an unblemished firstborn, for it is certainly speaking of an unblemished one, since it teaches: they graze until they become unfit.
rashi:a6.1: Actually in the present: and for this reason it grazes, since it is not fit for sacrifice, and he acquired it during its lifetime. And ours we give to the priests with their blemishes, for even though it has been blemished and is permitted to non-priests, there is still the prohibition of robbery. But with these comingled ones there is no prohibition of robbery, since each one says: I am a priest and I acquire it. It is money whose ownership is in doubt, and the burden of proof rests on the one who seeks to take from his fellow.
rashi:a9.1: Its animals: regarding the idolatrous city it is written: “And its animals, with the edge of the sword” (Deuteronomy 13:16). “Its animals” implies an animal that is its own, in which the Most High has no share.
rashi:a9.2: To exclude the money of second tithe in it: and this follows the one who says that second tithe is the property of the Most High.
rashi:a10.1: One designates an idolatrous city only, etc.: the reason is explained in the first chapter of Sanhedrin.
rashi:a11.1: This is “its animals”: for the priest eats the firstborn and the Israelite the tithe, and the Most High has no share in them.
rashi:a11.2: Well: for this reason a verse was needed to exclude it, since it is not excluded by “its spoil,” and not the spoils of Heaven; for this is not the spoils of Heaven, since the priest has acquired it. Another version: rather, it is obvious that it is speaking of an unblemished one, and [the verse] excludes it from the category of “its animals”; evidently it is the priest’s property. And this too is explained like the first version: since it was necessary to write “its animals” and it could not be derived from “its spoil,” learn from it that the priest has acquisition in it during its lifetime.
rashi:a14.1: To include offerings of lesser sanctity: that if he deposited a peace offering, a firstborn or a tithe animal with his fellow, and the fellow denied it, swore, and then admitted, he pays the principal and a fifth and brings the offering for an oath about a deposit, since they are [the depositor’s] property, and we apply to it “and deal falsely with his neighbor.”
rashi:a15.1: Ben Azzai says, to include peace offerings: he comes [to include them], since they are certainly his property; but not tithe, since it is not his property, as he may not sell it, whether alive or slaughtered, whether unblemished or blemished. And so it is explained in the chapter Arba’a Avot of Nezikin [Bava Kamma].
rashi:a15.2: Ben Azzai stated it only with regard to a firstborn: that [a priest] deposited [his firstborn] with another, who denied it and swore (and admitted). But peace offerings are not his property, since sanctity takes hold of them, as they require the laying on of hands, libations and the waving of the breast and thigh; nor is tithe, since he may not sell it. And so it is explained in the first chapter of Nezikin (Bava Kamma 12b).
rashi:a16.1: But it teaches it like peace offerings: and there are no peace offerings in the present.
rashi:a17.1: For if with a blemished one, it teaches it like peace offerings: and with peace offerings it certainly includes unblemished peace offerings, which are [their owner’s] property, since there is no misuse of consecrated property with them during their lifetime. For granted, with a priest’s firstborn one can distinguish between an unblemished one and a blemished one: with an unblemished one one can say that the priest acquires it only from the table of the Most High, that is, from the burning of the sacrificial portions, while a blemished one, which is not sacrificed, the Merciful One grants him immediately. But with an Israelite’s peace offerings one cannot say that the Israelite acquires them from the table of the Most High. Therefore, whether unblemished or blemished, he acquires them during their lifetime.
rashi:a17.2: Rather, is it not with an unblemished one: and it makes one who denies [having a firstborn] liable to the offering for an oath; evidently it is the priest’s property.
tosafot:a1.1: With regard to a firstborn it is stated, “you shall not redeem”: meaning that it always remains in its sanctity, in that it is not sold in the butchers’ market and not weighed by the litra.
tosafot:a1.2: Say the latter clause: “And you shall sprinkle their blood against the altar”: he is referring to the latter clause of the verse.
tosafot:a11.1: And with what? If we say with a blemished one, this is “its animals”: And if you say: let him say that it follows the Rabbis, who say that [a blemished firstborn] is not his property? One can say that the main difficulty is only from the tithe, for according to everyone a blemished one is his property. [So writes] the Rema [Rabbi Meir HaLevi Abulafia].
tosafot:a16.1: If we say in the present, but it teaches it like peace offerings: In the first chapter of Bava Kamma (12b) Rashi explained that it speaks of the time of the Temple because the verse about an oath concerning a deposit speaks of the time of the Temple, since that is when one is obligated to bring a guilt offering. And it seems that this is why [the Gemara] here uses “like peace offerings,” and did not want to say it as Rashi explained in Bava Kamma: because in any case it needs to say “like peace offerings” to prove that it speaks of an unblemished animal and not a blemished one, as we say shortly.
tosafot:b1.1: And it is Rabbi Shimon, who said: If unblemished ones came, they are sacrificed: but not at the outset. And the reason is that they have their support in their own place. Rabbi Akiva disagrees and says that even after the fact they are not sacrificed, and he explains the reason: because the firstborn is juxtaposed to the animal tithe, and the animal tithe to the grain tithe; just as the grain tithe is not brought from outside the Land to Eretz Yisrael, so too the firstborn and the tithe, etc. And if you say: why did [the Gemara] not establish it according to Rabbi Akiva, for whom it is all the more his property? One can say that according to Rabbi Akiva it is not so much like peace offerings.
tosafot:b6.1: No, they disagree in the dispute of Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva in our mishna: that is to say, and that one we established as a firstborn outside the Land.
tosafot:b7.1: Perhaps the Israelite will go and inflict a blemish on it, bring it (to his fellow) [to a halakhic authority] and say: A priest gave me this firstborn with its blemish: And if you say: what of it? They would not permit it to him, since the blemish came out of a priest’s hands without witnesses, for the priests were suspected of this. One can say that this is what he means: A priest gave it to me with its blemish, and before me the blemish befell it on its own. And if you say: how is there a concern that perhaps the Israelite will go and inflict a blemish on it? But Israelites are not suspected of this, as we say in Bekhorot (35a) that regarding a firstborn in an Israelite’s possession all are trusted, since it is the priests who are suspected about blemishes, but Israelites are not suspected. And one cannot say that this applies only to a definite firstborn, which he must eventually give to a priest, since an Israelite does not sin when it brings him nothing; for in the chapter Kol Pesulei HaMukdashin (Bekhorot 35b) Rav Naḥman said regarding an uncertain firstborn that its owners may testify about it. One can say that it is not comparable: that applies where it was unblemished at first in the Israelite’s possession; then he is afraid to inflict a blemish on it, since it was born in his domain and he has no way to slip out of [suspicion]. But here, where he can attribute it to the priest having given it to him with its blemish, he is to be suspected. And it seems that this is why [the Gemara] did not want to put it another way, that perhaps the Israelite will go and inflict a blemish on it and show it to a halakhic authority and say that it occurred by itself, without saying “a priest gave it to me”: in such a case he would not do so, lest they suspect him and say, why does he trouble himself over it and bring it to a halakhic authority, since it is not his? And [the Gemara] asks: But didn’t Rav Yehuda [our text of the Gemara: Rav] say: One does not examine a firstborn for an Israelite unless a priest is with him? And the reason is lest he keep it for himself and not give it to a priest. And since he must bring the priest, he cannot say, “A priest gave me this firstborn with its blemish,” for we tell him: Bring that priest who gave it to you; as long as he does not bring him, we do not permit the firstborn to him.
tosafot:b9.1: Rashi’s wording: This is the reason, because it looks like a priest who assists at the threshing floor: for it is common that one who sells a firstborn lowers the price for [an Israelite] so that he will give him a firstborn another time; and all the more so it is forbidden to receive it as a gift. And one must be careful: if an Israelite said to a priest, “Here is this firstborn,” and the priest said to him, “Let it be yours,” then it is forbidden to receive it, because it looks like a priest who assists at the threshing floor.
tosafot:b14.1: Rashi’s wording: This is the reason, because it looks like a priest who assists at the threshing floor: for it is common that one who sells a firstborn lowers the price for [an Israelite] so that he will give him a firstborn another time; and all the more so it is forbidden to receive it as a gift. And one must be careful: if an Israelite said to a priest, “Here is this firstborn,” and the priest said to him, “Let it be yours,” then it is forbidden to receive it, because it looks like a priest who assists at the threshing floor. [This note repeats, word for word, Tosafot’s note on Rav Huna’s statement above.]
gershom:a1.1: With regard to a firstborn it is stated, “you shall not redeem,” but it may be sold: for the priest sells it, since neither “it shall not be sold” nor “it shall not be redeemed” is written regarding it.
gershom:a2.1: Actually when the Temple is standing. And as for what is difficult for you, is there “and you shall sprinkle their blood”? Actually we are dealing with a blemished animal when the Temple is standing, and it is not difficult: the first clause of the verse, where it is written “you shall not redeem,” and we say that it may be sold, is with regard to a blemished animal, as is taught; and its latter clause, “and you shall sprinkle their blood,” is speaking of an unblemished one.
gershom:a3.1: The comingled ones grew up; they eat teruma either way, since each one says: If I am a priest, give to me for my own sake; if I am a priest’s slave, I am permitted to eat teruma.
gershom:a4.1: And they take one share in the granary, [since only one of them is a priest]. And it is taught concerning this that the firstborns of these comingled ones may not be sold, for only a definite priest may sell a firstborn; rather, they graze until they become unfit and are eaten with their blemish by the owners. For even though one of them is not a priest, he may eat it, since a firstborn with its blemish is not forbidden to an Israelite to eat; and no other priest can take it out of their [hands], since each one of them can say to him: Bring proof that I am not a priest, and take it.
gershom:a5.1: If in the present, what is different about ours and what is different about theirs? That is to say, all the firstborns of everyone also require blemishes, since they are eaten only with their blemishes.
gershom:a6.1: Rather, is it not speaking of when the Temple is standing? And granted, if you say that with ordinary firstborns of full priests the priest has acquisition in it, so that he can sell it, it is well: this is the difference between definite priests, ours, and these comingled ones, theirs, who cannot sell their firstborn; rather, it grazes until it becomes unfit. But if you say that priests have no acquisition in it to sell it, since it is not theirs but the altar’s, all the more so these, who are uncertain, have no acquisition in it at all; so let the treasurer come and take it and sacrifice it on the altar.
gershom:a7.1: Actually we are dealing [with the present]; and as for what you said, ours too require blemishes: there is a difference between ours and theirs, since our firstborns we give to the priest, but they [can] fend off the priest. The alternative version explains it more fully.
gershom:a8.1: [“Its animals,” written regarding the idolatrous city, where it is written “destroying it utterly, and all that is therein and its animals”: excluding an animal of firstborn and tithe in it, in which the Most High has a share.]
gershom:a9.1: If with a blemished firstborn, this is “its animals,” since the share of the Most High, for the altar, is disqualified. [And if you say that the priest has no acquisition in it and cannot sell it, because of the share of the Most High.]
gershom:a10.1: Why do I need “its animals”? To exclude the firstborn and tithe; derive the firstborn and tithe too from “its spoil,” and not the spoils of Heaven. Rather, since “its animals” was needed for the firstborn, learn from it that he has acquisition in it. And this is what it means: “its animals,” those that are particularly its own, in which the Most High has nothing, “and you shall burn,” excluding an animal of firstborn and tithe. And this is difficult for Rav Naḥman.
gershom:a11.1: Actually with a blemished one. And as for what is difficult for you, this is “its animals”: [it means] that which is eaten in the manner of “its animals,” as non-sacred meat, “and you shall burn”; the firstborn and tithe are excluded, as we learned, etc.
gershom:a12.1: To include offerings of lesser sanctity, which are their [owners’] property: in which the Most High and his fellow have a share, and he brings a guilt offering for misuse for them.
gershom:a13.1: Ben Azzai says, to include peace offerings. What does Ben Azzai exclude? He excludes tithe: since it is not sold, it is not considered his property.
gershom:a14.1: Abba Yosei ben Dosai says: Ben Azzai included only the firstborn alone: since it is sold unblemished while alive, it is his property. [And this is explained in Bava Kamma, in the first chapter.]
gershom:a15.1: But it teaches it like peace offerings: [this is] Abba Yosei; and peace offerings exist only when the Temple is standing.
gershom:a16.1: Rather, it is obvious, etc. But it teaches it like peace offerings, which can be sacrificed. Ravina said [our text has Abaye]: Actually, when the Temple is standing, and even so it is not difficult for Rav Naḥman. For here, which firstborn does Abba Yosei teach is his property, such that he can sell it? A firstborn that comes from outside the Land to the Land, and according to Rabbi Shimon, who said (below, in the chapter Elu Kodashim) [in Bava Kamma]: If unblemished ones came from outside the Land, they are sacrificed. If they came, yes; but at the outset one is (not) obligated [to bring them] and sacrifice them. Since it is so, that one is not obligated at the outset to bring them and sacrifice them, it is therefore his property and he can sell it. But a firstborn of Eretz Yisrael, which he must sacrifice, he cannot sell, as Rav Naḥman [said].
gershom:b1.1: What, is it not that this is what he is saying: the first tanna.
gershom:b2.1: In the house of a priest: he is saying that the owners do not render a substitute, but the priest does render a substitute; and since the priest renders a substitute, evidently he can sell it. And Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that once it has come into the hands of a priest no substitute is rendered, even by the priest, since he does not acquire it; and this accords with Rav Naḥman.
gershom:b3.1: No, these tanna’im disagree in the dispute of Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva. The first tanna, who said that in the house of a priest no substitute is rendered by the owners but [it is] by the priest, holds like Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri; Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds like Rabbi Akiva. Another version: with an Israelite a substitute is rendered. [Now according to this version, it implies that while it is in the Israelite’s domain even a priest may substitute with it, following the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who said that once it has come into a priest’s hands neither this one nor that one substitutes: by implication, with an Israelite both substitute with it; evidently he has acquisition in it. And the first tanna, who said that with an Israelite a substitute is rendered,] implies by the Israelite and not by the priest, and this accords with Rav Naḥman. [No, in the dispute, etc.]
gershom:b4.1: One does not examine a firstborn for an Israelite: when he comes and says, “A priest gave me this firstborn with its blemish.”
gershom:b5.1: Unless a priest was [with him]: who would say, “I gave it to him with its blemish.” And a priest sells to a priest, since the priest is not trusted on his own [word]. Rather, this is the reason it is forbidden to an Israelite: because it looks like a priest who assists [at the threshing floor]. [Just as to a priest who assists at the threshing floors teruma is not given, because it looks as though they give it to him as his wages, so too a priest who sells his firstborn to an Israelite looks as though he sells it to him cheaply so that, when a firstborn is born to him, he will give it to him and not to another; it is forbidden.]
gershom:b6.1: Another version: if you permit him to sell it to an Israelite, perhaps the Israelite will hold back the firstborn that is in his own flock until a blemish befalls it, and say: A priest sold me this firstborn with its blemish; and so he will slip out of it and not give his firstborn to a priest.
gershom:b7.1: And can he say this? But didn’t Rav Yehuda [our text: Rav] say, etc. [A marginal note in the printed edition suggests reading: unless a priest is with him and admits that the firstborn belongs to the Israelite.] (As “the first” is the firstborn.) [This last phrase is unclear in the printed text.]
gershom:b8.1: Mavrei: that it is healthier and fatter than others.
gershom:b9.1: They said to him: [There,] in the mishna, the matter proves itself, since [the priest] said to him within the period, [“Give it to me,” and he pays him nothing]; therefore it looks like a priest who assists [at the threshing floor], for it is through that benefit that he gives it to him, since he exempts him from tending it. Here, since he sells it and we give them money, it does not look like a priest who assists.
gershom:b10.1: What would you say, perhaps the priest lowers the price for him, giving it to him for less than its value? He would not do so, since he thinks: a zucchini is better than a gourd. Better the small profit that I take now, selling it to him at its value, than to take less now for the sake of a later profit. Another version: Mar Zutra, etc. They said to him: We do not hold [like Rav Huna]; and further, we are buying it. He said to them: And do you not hold the mishna, which accords with Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua? They said to him: It is not comparable, for there the matter proves itself, since he gives it to him without payment; but here we are buying it, and it does not look like a priest who assists.
rashi:b1.1: Actually with an unblemished one: and it is not difficult for Rav Naḥman, for where the priest acquires it during its lifetime, we are dealing with a firstborn outside the Land, which ordinarily does not stand for sacrifice, even when the Temple is standing. And it is like peace offerings, in that if he brings it he may sacrifice it, but ordinarily it does not stand for sacrifice.
rashi:b1.2: And it is Rabbi Shimon: who says below in the chapter Elu Kodashim (Temurah 21a): If unblemished firstborns came from outside the Land, they are sacrificed. If they came, yes; at the outset, no.
rashi:b2.1: It speaks of it like a sin offering and a guilt offering: and this sin offering and guilt offering are unblemished ones, since it teaches that the priests do not acquire them during their lifetime, but after slaughter they do acquire them; evidently we are dealing with animals fit for sacrifice.
rashi:b4.1: Let us say it is a dispute between tanna’im: whether the priest acquires an unblemished firstborn during its lifetime when the Temple is standing, or not.
rashi:b5.1: What, is it not that this is what he is saying: the first tanna [means]: in the priest’s house no substitute is rendered by the owners, but by the priest; for the priest does substitute with it, since he has acquisition in it.
rashi:b6.1: No: they disagree in the dispute of Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva in our mishna, and that one we have established as a firstborn outside the Land. And the first tanna says that the priest renders a substitute with it once it has come into his hands, since he acquires it during its lifetime, as it ordinarily does not stand for sacrifice, like Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri. And Rabbi Shimon is like Rabbi Akiva: even though [the priest] has acquisition in it, no substitute is rendered by him, since [Rabbi Akiva] derives it from the juxtaposition, as explained in the mishna: “Where does the sanctity take effect on it,” etc. [The note ends with a short, cryptic gloss, apparently on the baraita’s wording:] “They render a substitute”: of the Israelite; “and the priest does not render a substitute”: neither this one nor that one.
rashi:b6.2: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, etc., this one and that one [Rashi’s text of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar’s words reads “neither this one nor that one renders a substitute,” where the English above has “its owner”]: the priest and the Israelite. What, is it not that Rav Naḥman’s [ruling] is the difference between them: that what the first tanna says, that with the priest no substitute is rendered [by the owner] since [the priest] has acquisition in it, is “like Rav Naḥman,” and Rabbi Shimon does not hold Rav Naḥman’s [view]? No: all agree in not holding Rav Naḥman’s [view] with a proper firstborn, and here they disagree in the dispute of Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva, with a firstborn outside the Land; and that is why the first tanna said that the priest does not render a substitute with it, and Rabbi Shimon is like Rabbi Akiva. Another version: Let us say it is a dispute between tanna’im: a firstborn with a priest has no substitute rendered for it, neither by the Israelite nor by the priest. And we say: it is substituting that he may not do, but he may sell it. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: Once it has come into the priest’s hands, neither this one nor that one renders a substitute; that is to say, he may not even sell it, since each later tanna comes to add something. What, is it not that Rav Naḥman’s [ruling] is the difference between them: the first tanna holds Rav Naḥman’s [view], and Rabbi [Shimon ben] Elazar does not hold Rav Naḥman’s [view]? [So the printed text reads in both versions, although by the Gemara’s reasoning above it is the first tanna who holds that the priest acquires the firstborn.]
rashi:b7.1: They taught this only of a priest to a priest: he may sell it unblemished.
rashi:b7.2: A priest gave me this firstborn with its blemish: but with a priest to a priest one cannot say this, since a priest who brings a firstborn to show a halakhic authority must bring witnesses that the blemish befell it by itself. As we say in Bekhorot, in the chapter Kol Pesulei HaMukdashin (Bekhorot 35a): with all blemishes that can be caused by a person, Israelite herdsmen are trusted and priestly herdsmen are not trusted, since priests were suspected regarding firstborns.
rashi:b8.1: And may a halakhic authority permit it so: even if it is a permanent blemish, may a halakhic authority permit the firstborn to an Israelite without a priest with him?
rashi:b8.2: Unless a priest is with him: for perhaps, when this one knows that it is a permanent blemish, so that it is no longer [a case of] consecrated animals [slaughtered] outside [the Temple], he will eat it and not worry about robbing the priest. Therefore we require a priest with him, and he cannot say, “A priest gave me this firstborn with its blemish,” since we tell him: Bring me that priest who gave it to you. As long as he does not bring him, we do not permit the firstborn to him unless a priest gave it to him.
rashi:b9.1: This is the reason it is forbidden to an Israelite: to buy an unblemished firstborn from the priest: because an unblemished firstborn in the present is ordinarily sold cheaply, since the buyer must keep it until it is blemished. Therefore this priest who lowers the price for an Israelite looks like a priest who assists at the threshing floors, winnowing and binding sheaves, so that they will give him the terumot; and it is a desecration of God’s name, for it looks like one who takes teruma as wages. And this priest too looks as though he lowers the price for the Israelite for this reason, so that he will give him the firstborns that will be born in his flock.
rashi:b10.1: Let the Master eat, for it is healthful: for the meat of a firstborn is healthier to eat than other meat.
rashi:b10.2: From where do you have this: who gave it to you? You are not priests.
rashi:b11.1: And do you not hold: that it is forbidden to buy the meat of a firstborn from a priest, lest he lower the price for you, and it looks like a priest who assists?
rashi:b11.2: We are buying it: and there is no concern of [his being one who] assists, since he did not give it to us as a gift.
rashi:b12.1: To tend: to take trouble over it, raising it, before he gives it to the priest.
rashi:b12.2: Like a priest who assists: for this now is assistance, that he saves him from the trouble of it, only so that he will give it to him.
rashi:b13.1: The matter proves: that he is one who assists, for he immediately saves him from the trouble and the feeding.
rashi:b14.1: What would you say, perhaps the priest lowers the price: so that he will give him our firstborns and not another priest.
rashi:b14.2: No: he does not do so.
rashi:b14.3: For he considers: a butzina now is better than a kara tomorrow. A butzina is a small gourd; a kara is a large gourd. That is to say: better that I sell it at its value, for perhaps if I leave them some of the price it will gain me nothing, and they will not give me their firstborns.
